dude · Talking to a task

Mockup for docs/design/conductor.md, on the design system's real tokens.css (dude main @ 8e3ef2c). Every task gets one conversation, the Chat tab. On the other end is the task's conductor, an agent with its own face and the orchestrator role's colour. It plans with you, starts the same phase Runs Deliver starts, reads what they did with dude diff, steers them, makes small edits itself, and asks before the PR. El Duderino is dude's own voice in the chat: he writes the first prompt and the wake notes, posts GitHub's news, and says when the conductor parks. He tells the conductor what happened; the conductor decides what to do. Asking about a finished PR is the same chat, resumed.

1 · Starting a task

"How would I start a task with this agent, instead of automatic delivering?"

A task that hasn't started shows two ways to start where the "Not started" empty state is today, side by side and equal: you pick each time, and no project setting picks for you. Abide starts the conductor in the Chat tab, to talk it through with you; El Duderino gives it the goal and criteria as its first prompt. Roll is today's automatic pipeline, unchanged: let it go and it runs to the PR on its own. Either way you can always type in Chat: the first message on a rolling task starts its conductor and hands it the task's decisions (section 5).

How to start

Abide

Talk it through. The conductor reads the task and the code, asks what it needs, proposes a plan, and runs the agents with you watching.

  • You can interrupt any time, and it steers the agents for you, or makes a small change itself
  • It decides the review rounds and the simplifier with you
  • It waits for your go before opening the PR
Conductor · claude-opus-5-5 · Small

Roll

Deliver straight through: implementer, reviewers, fixer, simplifier, then the PR. Nobody needs to be here.

  • Stops only on a question or an escalation
  • You can still open Chat later and take over

2 · Planning together

The first minutes of a talked-through task

The Chat tab is a normal transcript (ChatTranscript, ChatMessage, QuestionCard, ChatComposer). The first turn is El Duderino's, the task's dude name in the system style the design system already gives prompts: dude writes it from the task, as it writes every phase prompt today. The conductor reads before it asks. Its question is a real QuestionCard: the task goes to "Waiting on you" in the sidebar, and the conductor stays warm for a while, then parks, so it holds no host while you think.

3 · Conducting and steering

"How would it conduct the other agents? How would it steer their work?"

The conductor starts phase Runs: the same implementer, reviewers and simplifier dude already has, each in its own lux container and checkout, handing off through git exactly as now. Each one appears nested in the chat as a thread (ChatThread, with a rail in the agent's role colour) that shows a one-line status, collapses, and opens the full session. Between turns the conductor is warm for a few minutes, then parked: no host, no model tokens. When something happens, El Duderino wakes it with one note of facts (which Run, its commit, how many files and lines, tests, findings by severity) and never a diff: the conductor reads what it needs with dude diff. When you say something mid-run, the conductor decides who needs it and steers that agent, or, for a small thing, does it itself.

4 · The PR gate

The PR is the last step, and it waits for you

The conductor can't open a PR on its own. The workflow parks before openPullRequest; the conductor's decide("open the pull request") is refused until you've said so in the chat. Before it asks, it says what ran and what didn't. Nothing reaches GitHub before this except the per-Run handoff branches.

5 · After the PR, including tasks you didn't run

"How would I start a chat with it after the PR has already been made?"

You just type in Chat. Every task has one, including tasks that were Delivered automatically or finished weeks ago. When nobody has talked to it yet, the tab shows the pipeline as a compact history, with an empty composer underneath. Your first message starts the task's conductor, briefed from what dude already has: the task, every Run's outcome, the findings and how each was settled, the PRs and their feedback. It reads more with tools and answers with links to the evidence. On a running Delivered task, the step in flight finishes and the next decision is the conductor's ("Let Deliver finish it" hands it back). On a merged task it is read-only: a change becomes a linked follow-up task. This is the "ask agent" too: same chat, same agent.

A stream can only be read once, and after the first attempt it's spent. Retrying would send an empty body. The implementer found this in its own tests (session turn 12); retry.ts:58 checks body instanceof ReadableStream. Answered from the task's history; no change made.

6 · Where it lives in the task's current UI

"How would a conversation with this agent be displayed in the task's current UI?"

One new tab, Chat, first in the bar; nothing else moves. The README already says "Chat is the primary surface", and the Chat tab is where a task opens once it has a conversation (Overview until then). Sessions stays the drill-down: the conductor goes at the top, and the agents it started are indented under it, like SessionTree; a Delivered task's earlier Runs sit under "Delivered automatically". Opening one is today's session view, composer included, so you can still steer an agent directly (the conductor sees that you did). The header's face shows the conductor on the owner while it works, the same pattern as the implementer today.

What each surface shows

  • Chat: the conversation with the conductor. Its messages, yours, its questions, El Duderino's prompts and wake notes in the system style, and each agent as a collapsed ChatThread. Tool calls (dude diff, its edits) stay in a ChatAside like any session.
  • Chat rail: Team (who's running, parked, done), Plan (the gates, with the PR locked until you say go), and cost.
  • Overview → Pipeline: unchanged. The conductor's Runs are ordinary phase Runs, so the step list, Findings, Files, Servers and Activity all work without changes.
  • Sidebar: a waiting conductor question puts the task in "Waiting on you", as ask_person does now. A parked conductor shows nothing: parked is quiet.
  • Mobile / narrow: the rail folds away, as the session rail does below ~820px; the thread headers keep status and cost.

7 · How it works

The pipeline stays; the conductor takes its decisions

  • The delivery workflow keeps the mechanics: start phase Runs, wait for all of them, advance the branch, open PRs, classify GitHub. With State.Decider = conductor, each decision point parks on a conductor decision instead of applying the policy: after implement, after a review round (triage), after a fix, before the PR, on PR feedback, on an escalation.
  • Its tools (agenttools): start_phase (the same CreatePhaseRun), steer (a directive), dude diff (built, #33), findings / dismiss_finding, pull_requests, decide, ask_person (built).
  • Policy bounds stay: review iterations, attempts per finding, PR fix rounds. Past one, it must ask you.
  • A lux Run like any agent, with role conductor (the orchestrator enum value, renamed) and its own settings: model, effort, machine. Its machine is small: it reads, edits and talks; anything that runs the code is a phase Run.
  • Warm for conductorWarmMinutes after a turn, then parked (dude_pause='conductor'); a wake resumes it with its conversation.

Wakes, and its checkout

  • Woken for a decision or a person; never for an approval, a green check, or one reviewer of four. Wake reasons that land together are one turn.
  • El Duderino's note is fixed-size facts and ids, never a diff or a file list: the conductor pulls those with dude diff, files first.
  • Its checkout is kept current by lux: on every wake, lux's runner fetches the task's heads and drops a git bundle in; git fast-forwards inside. No credential in the container; lux still never runs git in the checkout.
  • Its edits publish like a phase, one writer at a time, and only small ones (60 lines, 3 files; past it, "delegate this"). It cannot test them, so a conductor edit is never the last thing before the PR: a review or test Run must have run on that head.

Order of work

  1. Measure a lux resume, end to end.
  2. Read-only Chat on any task: the conductor Run, briefing, dude diff, warm-then-parked, El Duderino's notes.
  3. Decisions: the decider switch, start_phase / decide, coalesced wakes, Abide, taking over, the PR gate.
  4. Steering: steer, and lux delivering it mid-turn.
  5. GitHub: routing to the conductor, @dude, webhooks when a project's repositories are added.
  6. Edits: lux's incoming bundle, the conductor's publish and its limit.

Still open

  • The verbs: Abide / Roll, or another pair?
  • The small machine's numbers (proposed: 0.5 CPU · 1 GiB · 10 GiB).
